PROCUREMENT / 6 MIN READ

What to include in a custom screw RFQ

A useful quotation starts with a clear specification. A drawing is the best starting point, but a sample, sketch or assembly description can also help define the next questions.

ZUFEK Technical Resources • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEStart with the drawing and revisionIdentify the features that matterSpecify material and finish separatelyInclude quantity and delivery contextYour RFQ checklist
RELATED PRODUCTCustom Metal Screws ↗

Start with the drawing and revision

Include the drawing number, revision, units and quantity. Show overall length, thread specification, head dimensions and any shoulders. If a requirement is still open, label it as open rather than leaving it ambiguous.

Identify the features that matter

Mark dimensions that affect fit or function. Explain the mating part, assembly access and service conditions. A tolerance on every surface may create unnecessary cost; let functional needs guide the discussion.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom metal screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Specify material and finish separately

State a material grade if it is known. Identify any coating, appearance or corrosion requirements separately. A material family or a finish name alone may not be enough to define an acceptance requirement.

Include quantity and delivery context

Provide prototype quantity, initial order quantity and expected repeat demand if available. Include the destination and requested date. Lead time and feasibility need confirmation after technical review.

Your RFQ checklist

Drawing or sketch • revision and units • material • finish • critical features • quantity • inspection documents • destination. Downloading a checklist is optional: you can paste these details directly into the quotation form.

Ready to discuss your part?

Use the RFQ preparation checklist, then submit your drawing for review. For acceptance requirements, see quality planning.

DESIGN & DIMENSIONS / 7 MIN READ

A practical guide to shoulder screw drawings

The shoulder, thread and head work together as one geometry. A clear drawing explains not only the dimensions, but also which surfaces locate, rotate or clamp in your assembly.

ZUFEK Technical Resources • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEDefine the shoulderShow how the thread endsReview head access and seatingCommunicate functional tolerances
RELATED PRODUCTShoulder Screws ↗

Define the shoulder

Dimension shoulder diameter and shoulder length independently from thread length. Explain whether the shoulder serves as a locating surface, bearing surface or spacer. The functional role helps identify which features need closer review.

Show how the thread ends

State thread designation and length, and show any relief or transition at the shoulder. Check how the screw seats in the mating assembly. Do not assume the end of the usable thread is identical to the end of the visible thread form.

Working on this type of part? Explore our shoulder screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Review head access and seating

Include head diameter, height and drive configuration. Consider the tool clearance and seating surface in the assembly. A head that fits the drawing may still be inaccessible once neighboring parts are installed.

Communicate functional tolerances

Mark the mating bore relationship and any surface finish requirement that affects motion or fit. Tolerances should be established by the application engineer and confirmed during manufacturing review.

Ready to discuss your part?

Use the RFQ preparation checklist, then submit your drawing for review. For acceptance requirements, see quality planning.

DESIGN & DIMENSIONS / 5 MIN READ

Five questions before specifying a captive screw

A captive screw is part of a retention system. Review the panel, retaining feature and mating thread together before finalizing the screw drawing.

ZUFEK Technical Resources • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEWhat retains the screw?How much movement is needed?What happens during service?How will the assembly be verified?What should accompany the RFQ?
RELATED PRODUCTCaptive Screws ↗

What retains the screw?

Describe the intended retaining component or geometry. Provide an assembly view and panel details. The screw alone does not establish whether the completed assembly will remain captive.

How much movement is needed?

Show required travel, open position and thread engagement. Explain how the operator installs and releases the fastener, including available access.

Working on this type of part? Explore our captive screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

What happens during service?

Describe repeated access, vibration, cleaning and exposure conditions. These inputs inform the material, finish and design discussion; they do not replace assembly testing.

How will the assembly be verified?

Define retention and functional acceptance criteria with your engineering team. A dimensional inspection and an assembly test answer different questions.

What should accompany the RFQ?

Include the screw drawing, mating assembly, quantity and any sample photos. Unresolved retention details can be reviewed before a final quotation is issued.

Choosing material for a custom metal screw

Material selection begins with the service environment and mechanical requirements. The best specification balances function, manufacturability, availability and verification.

ZUFEK Technical Resources • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEDescribe the environment firstDefine the mechanical requirementsTreat finish as part of the systemConfirm documentation needs
RELATED PRODUCTCustom Metal Screws ↗

Describe the environment first

State whether the part will encounter moisture, chemicals, heat or outdoor exposure. Include contact with dissimilar metals and any cleaning process. Avoid choosing a grade based on appearance alone.

Define the mechanical requirements

Provide the applicable strength, hardness or other performance requirements where relevant. Different grades and processing conditions can behave differently; a material family alone is not a complete mechanical specification.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom metal screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Treat finish as part of the system

Coatings may influence dimensions, friction and assembly behavior. Identify the required finish and the surfaces on which it matters. Allowances should be reviewed against the drawing and actual process.

Confirm documentation needs

Tell the supplier whether you require material documentation, inspection records or other supporting evidence. Confirm availability and acceptance requirements before placing an order.

What affects the price of a non-standard screw?

A custom screw quotation reflects the complete specification and order conditions. Understanding the cost drivers can make a design review more productive.

ZUFEK Technical Resources • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEGeometry and manufacturing routeTolerance and inspectionMaterial, finish and order volumeDiscuss changes before revising
RELATED PRODUCTSpecial Head Screws ↗

Geometry and manufacturing route

Head shape, length ratios, steps, internal features and thread configuration affect the manufacturing options. Feasibility needs review against the actual drawing and available processes.

Tolerance and inspection

Tighter requirements can change processing and measurement effort. Identify truly critical dimensions so the review focuses on the features that drive function.

Working on this type of part? Explore our special head screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

Material, finish and order volume

Material grade, secondary operations, finish requirements and batch size affect the quotation. Prototype and repeat production quantities may have different cost structures.

Discuss changes before revising

Ask which drawing features influence cost. Any proposed change should be reviewed and approved by the responsible engineer before manufacturing. A lower quoted price is only useful if the part still meets the application requirements.

How to prepare an inspection plan for custom screws

An inspection plan translates a drawing into agreed checks and records. Define it during the quotation stage so acceptance is understood before production.

ZUFEK Technical Resources • Published October 29, 2026
IN THIS GUIDEUse the current drawingIdentify critical characteristicsAgree on methods and recordsPlan sample approval
RELATED PRODUCTShoulder Screws ↗

Use the current drawing

Link the inspection plan to the drawing number and revision. Resolve unclear notes and conflicting requirements before the part is released.

Identify critical characteristics

List the dimensions, thread requirements, material and finish characteristics to be verified. Distinguish dimensional checks from functional assembly checks.

Agree on methods and records

Discuss measurement methods, sampling requirements and required reporting. Equipment suitability and acceptance criteria should be agreed for the actual features involved.

Plan sample approval

Where required, confirm how samples will be identified, reviewed and approved. Record approved changes so repeat orders refer to the same specification.
